title: Conditionals and loops
runtime: Modern evergreen browser or Node.js with ES modules. Run fragments in browser DevTools or a small .js file unless the example says otherwise.

objectives.text: Choose code with if, else, and switch.
Repeat work with the right loop.
Use break, continue, and return deliberately.
Prevent infinite loops and off-by-one errors.

learningFlow: Explain the result in your own words
Apply the idea in a different problem
Review after two and seven days

diagnostic.question: Can you explain the main purpose of conditionals and loops before reading?
diagnostic.answer: A complete answer should name the problem it solves, the values or control flow involved, and one mistake to avoid.

sections.title: Conditionals choose a path
sections.body: if runs a block when its condition is truthy; else if tests another path and else handles what remains. switch is useful when one value is compared with several exact cases. Include breaks unless fall-through is intentional. Keep conditions about decisions and move complex work into well-named functions.

sections.title: Loops repeat with control
sections.body: for is useful when initialization, condition, and update belong together. for...of reads iterable values such as array items; for...in reads enumerable property keys and is usually not the right array loop. while fits repetition whose end depends on a changing condition rather than a known collection.

sections.title: Stopping and skipping
sections.body: break ends the nearest loop or switch. continue skips the rest of the current loop iteration. return ends the whole function and can return a value. Choose the smallest control tool that matches the intent, because hidden exits make a long loop hard to reason about.

sections.title: Prove that a loop ends
sections.body: A loop needs a condition that eventually becomes false. For an array, valid indexes run from 0 through length - 1, so i < items.length is a common boundary. Trace the first, last, and empty cases by hand before trusting the loop.

sections.title: Why this matters in React
sections.body: Conditionals and loops is part of the JavaScript model React code already uses. Components, event handlers, state updates, list rendering, and data requests become easier to reason about when this concept is understood without framework shortcuts. Practise the JavaScript behavior first, then identify the same rule in JSX or a component.

interviewQuestions.question: Explain conditionals and loops to a junior developer.
interviewQuestions.answer: Choose code with if, else, and switch. Repeat work with the right loop. Use break, continue, and return deliberately. Prevent infinite loops and off-by-one errors.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Show a small example and one common mistake.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you prove that code using conditionals and loops behaves correctly?
interviewQuestions.answer: State the expected value or control flow first, test normal and boundary cases, and inspect the actual runtime result. Explain the JavaScript rule behind the evidence.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Which edge case would you test first?

interviewQuestions.question: Where can conditionals and loops affect React code?
interviewQuestions.answer: It can affect values, callbacks, rendering decisions, updates, or data flow. The exact connection depends on the concept; the important step is to reason from JavaScript behavior before blaming React.

mastery.policy: Reading or opening a solution is guided exposure, not mastery. Save an attempt, solve again without help, explain the rule, and transfer it to a new problem.

commonMistakes.symptom: Code using conditionals and loops produces a surprising value.
commonMistakes.cause: The result was run before the value, type, scope, identity, or control flow was predicted.
commonMistakes.fix: Reduce the case, write the expected result, and apply the exact rule from the matching section.

commonMistakes.symptom: A learner copies syntax but cannot adapt it.
commonMistakes.cause: The example was memorized without explaining why it works.
commonMistakes.fix: Change the data and names, predict again, and explain which behavior must stay the same.

commonMistakes.symptom: A React problem is blamed on React immediately.
commonMistakes.cause: The underlying JavaScript behavior was not isolated first.
commonMistakes.fix: Reproduce the value or function behavior in a small JavaScript example, then reconnect it to the component.
